extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators (plaintiffs and defendants) handling computer-based patent cases in U.S. federal courts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for litigants on using Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) motions to dismiss Section 101 (Alice) challenges to computer-based patent claims, including venue choice, claim-construction tactics, and briefing strategies. Focused on maximizing chances of early case disposition while avoiding pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility under Alice
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to abstract ideas alone are not patent-eligible under the Supreme Court’s decision in Alice Corp. Pty. Ltd. v. CLS Bank Int’l.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice remains the controlling standard for subject-matter eligibility of computer-based claims; motions to dismiss based on Section 101 press this ground early in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical likelihood of Rule 12 success (post-Alice trend)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the number of Section 101-based motions to dismiss has increased, the rate at which courts grant dismissal has decreased (from 71% in 2015 to 53% in 2016 in the sampled decisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these empirical trends to set expectations: motions remain a plausible early-disposition tool, but success is not as high as in the immediate post-Alice period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue selection based on historical grant rates
rubrics_metrics.description: The grant rate for Section 101 motions varies substantially by jurisdiction; the most active venues for computer-related eligibility motions are D. Del., E.D. Tex., and C.D. Cal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on analyzed decisions: best chance of succeeding on a Rule 12 motion is in the District of Delaware; best chance at summary judgment is in the Central District of California; the Eastern District of Texas has been least receptive to Rule 12. Litigants should consider these venue-specific histories when deciding where to file or whether to move to dismiss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low cost/early-resolution attractiveness of Rule 12 motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the cost of bringing motions to dismiss is relatively low, defendants are likely to continue filing Section 101 challenges early in cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants can avoid high discovery costs and legal fees with a successful motion to dismiss, making early motions an attractive strategic option even if overall grant rates have fallen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction can be dispositive for Section 101 at the motion stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts denying Section 101 motions often determine that claim construction — defining the scope and meaning of a patent — is necessary to resolve the Section 101 challenge, or they dismiss without prejudice to developing Section 101 arguments later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs can try to persuade courts to require claim construction to sidestep Alice; doing so requires showing a genuine dispute over claim scope and may benefit from specific, detailed constructions supported by expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices for plaintiffs relying on claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The best chance of success for patent owners tends to be portraying a fundamental dispute over the basic character and coverage of the patent claims and/or adopting a specific and detailed claim construction argument based on expert testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs should propose concrete constructions and tie them to factual disputes and expert support; avoid vague assertions that construction is needed without particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitfalls when invoking claim construction to avoid Section 101
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants may portray claim-construction arguments as an improper attempt to sidestep the Alice analysis, or may accept a plaintiff’s proposed construction and still argue invalidity under Section 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs risk having their proposed constructions accepted and then losing on Section 101 anyway; defendants can neutralize construction-based defenses by agreeing to constructions and proceeding to eligibility analysis. Be prepared for these counter-moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of factual analogy to Federal Circuit precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties should devote a significant portion of their written submissions to showing how their case is analogous to (or distinguishable from) the limited number of post-Alice Federal Circuit decisions that have found computer-based claims to be valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-thirds of district-court cases finding computer-based claims valid at the motion-to-dismiss stage explicitly analogized the factual content of the claims or the plaintiff’s rationale to Federal Circuit decisions. Use close factual comparisons (or distinctions) in briefs to persuade courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant strategy: minimize claim construction and emphasize factual distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement defendants should focus on minimizing issues of claim construction and instead factually distinguish the asserted claims from those in Federal Circuit opinions that found eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving plaintiffs an opportunity to convert the motion into a claim-construction dispute; instead press factual differences and abstract-idea character to support invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early post-Alice challenges targeted the most vulnerable patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial post-Alice decisions often involved patents that were extremely susceptible to challenges (analogous to early IPRs which targeted vulnerable patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should recognize that early-filed Section 101 motions may have been aimed at weak patents; current motions may face comparatively stronger patents, explaining the decline in grant rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low risk of raising Section 101 early in litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little risk of bringing Section 101 challenges early in the litigation, as courts rarely find patents eligible at the motion-to-dismiss stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because courts infrequently find patents eligible at Rule 12, defendants can bring early eligibility challenges without substantial downside; plaintiffs should assess vulnerabilities early and consider defenses accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: When courts deny motions, they often preserve later development
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts that deny Section 101 motions at the motion-to-dismiss stage commonly do so because claim construction or factual development is required, or they dismiss without prejudice to revisiting Section 101 later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect denials to result in further claim-construction briefing or development of the factual record; craft briefing to either push for immediate eligibility resolution or to preserve arguments for later stages.
